tldr: A reinforcement learning framework for humanoids to instantly dodge incoming obstacles using whole-body motions and recover balance without falling. Deployed on real hardware (PM01), it successfully evaded balls traveling at dozens of kilometers per hour (up to 10 m/s) using steps and ducking maneuvers.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of Humanoid Dodgeball. Evasive rewards are derived from threat computation based on link-wise collision predictions, while direction-specific adversarial motion priors (AMP) promote diverse, human-like evasive motions tailored to the intended escape direction. Once the threat clears, a capture point reward restores the robot to a stable standing posture.
overview:
Humanoid dynamic locomotion has advanced dramatically in recent years, mastering intense behaviors such as parkour and soccer. However, dodging fast-flying balls and obstacles on the fly remains a daunting hurdle. While quadrupedal robots and drones can simply translate their chassis or adjust their speed, humanoids have limited base support. They must coordinate high-degree-of-freedom whole-body motions while carefully maintaining center-of-mass balance.

To tackle this, the authors developed "Humanoid Dodgeball," a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for agile obstacle dodging. It introduces three core innovations: First, it geometrically calculates "predictive threat" (when and where a collision will occur) and "near-field threat" (current proximity) across major body links, embedding these into threat-aware reward shaping. Second, it uses separate direction-specific Adversarial Motion Prior (AMP) discriminators for each evasion direction (forward, backward, left, right), unlocking diverse, human-like reactions such as stepping forward or ducking instead of solely retreating. Third, it introduces a capture point reward based on the linear inverted pendulum model (LIPM) to prevent falls and restore upright posture after dodging.

In simulation, the method was validated on two humanoid platforms—Unitree G1 and EngineAI PM01—achieving dodge success rates that significantly outperform recent baselines (PAC-MAN and REBot). Furthermore, in real-world experiments on the PM01 robot tracked with motion capture, the robot successfully dodged incoming balls thrown at 3 to 10 m/s in 73% of trials (22 out of 30) through coordinated stepping and ducking maneuvers while remaining upright.
contributions: A threat-aware reward design that geometrically evaluates threat levels using predicted time-to-collision and required avoidance acceleration across whole-body links, driving precise evasive motions.
Four independent direction-specific AMP discriminators (forward, backward, left, right) that prevent behavioral bias toward single patterns and foster diverse, natural evasive movements.
Integration of a linear inverted pendulum-based capture point objective, enabling rapid balance recovery and upright stabilization immediately after aggressive whole-body dodging.
Demonstrated feasibility of whole-body coordinated evasion across two simulated platforms (G1, PM01) and real-world PM01 ball-throwing experiments at speeds between 3 and 10 m/s.

sections.heading: Dodging incoming threats on the fly: The ultimate humanoid frontier
sections.summary: Although humanoids have become increasingly agile, evading fast dynamic obstacles remains an open challenge. Robots must react instantly under high-dimensional whole-body dynamics and strict balance constraints. This work proposes an evasion learning framework combining threat-aware rewards with direction-specific motion priors.
sections.details:
Through reinforcement learning with large-scale human motion data, humanoids have mastered sophisticated skills like soccer, tennis, and parkour. Research into safety-critical behaviors, such as fall damage mitigation and static obstacle navigation, has also progressed.

Yet, evading incoming airborne projectiles—a basic survival instinct for humans and animals—remains extremely difficult for robots. Drones can accelerate away in three dimensions, and quadrupeds can shift laterally over a wide support polygon. Humanoids, by contrast, rely on bipedal support. Simply shifting the body sideways can lead to an immediate fall. The robot must tuck its head or torso, execute coordinated foot placement, and continuously stabilize its center of mass upon landing.

To overcome these hurdles, this paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework named "Humanoid Dodgeball." Combining rewards that explicitly assess projectile threats, adversarial motion priors (AMP) dedicated to specific escape headings, and capture-point stabilization rewards, the system achieves agile and physically feasible whole-body evasive maneuvers.

sections.heading: Why humanoid evasion is fundamentally harder than drones or quadrupeds
sections.summary: Dynamic obstacle avoidance has been explored in drones and quadrupeds, but those solutions do not translate well to humanoid constraints. While a concurrent humanoid evasion method (PAC-MAN) emerged recently, it suffered from directional bias and overfitting to limited trajectories.
sections.details:
Agile obstacle evasion has historically been studied on drones and quadrupeds.

- On drones: Methods like artificial potential fields using ultra-low-latency event cameras and end-to-end RL over LiDAR point clouds have enabled high-speed projectile dodging.
- On quadrupeds: Frameworks such as ABS (switching agile locomotion and recovery policies via value functions) and REBot (reflexive evasion governed by state machines) achieve rapid whole-body avoidance.

However, these strategies cannot be directly applied to humanoids. Humanoids possess many more degrees of freedom (DoF) and tiny foot contact areas, meaning simple base velocity commands or planar translations are insufficient.

Concurrently, a humanoid avoidance framework named PAC-MAN was proposed, combining control barrier function (CBF)-inspired rewards with AMP. However, PAC-MAN evaluated only restricted projectile paths and suffered from directional collapse—almost exclusively stepping backward—limiting its generalization. The proposed framework overcomes these shortcomings by handling a broader spectrum of approach angles and projectile velocities.

sections.heading: A learning architecture unifying threat estimation, directional AMP, and capture points
sections.summary: By modeling 10 body links and the obstacle as spheres, the system computes predictive and near-field threats from time-to-collision and required acceleration. Four direction-specific AMP discriminators produce natural and diverse evasive styles, while capture point tracking guarantees stable recovery after dodging.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
Dynamic obstacle avoidance is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). The policy observation $\bm{o}_t$ includes robot proprioception (base angular velocity, roll and pitch angles, joint positions and velocities, and previous action) alongside the obstacle's 3D relative position $[x^o, y^o, z^o]$ in the base frame. Actions $\bm{a}_t$ are joint position target offsets relative to a default standing pose, mapped to motor torques via PD controllers. A fall (any non-foot link touching the ground) is marked as a failure.

### III-B Threat-Aware Reward Design
Ten key robot links (head, torso, upper and lower links of both arms, and upper and lower links of both legs) and the obstacle are modeled as bounding spheres.
- Predictive Threat: Assuming linear motion, the closest approach time $\tau_t^{i*}$ and closest distance $d_t^{i*}$ are calculated from relative positions and velocities. The required acceleration $a_{\mathrm{req},t}^i$ to escape the collision sphere is mapped to a normalized threat metric $S_t^i \in [0, 1]$ relative to a reference acceleration $a_{\mathrm{ref}}=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
- Near-field Threat: Proximity clearance $c_t^i$ is mapped into $D_t^i \in [0, 1]$ using a Gaussian kernel.
Based on these metrics, the reward includes a body-escape reward $r_t^{\mathrm{escape}}$ encouraging velocities away from predicted collision points, a distance clearance penalty $r_t^{\mathrm{distance}}$, and a root-escape direction reward $r_t^{\mathrm{root-dir}}$ guiding coordinated horizontal base displacement. Once the threat clears, a capture point reward $r_t^{\mathrm{capture}}$ based on the linear inverted pendulum model penalizes the offset between the capture point $\bm{p}^{\mathrm{capture}}$ and the support polygon center, preventing post-dodge falls.

### III-C Direction-Specific Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP)
Using a single AMP discriminator tends to bias the policy toward frequent actions like backward retreats. To prevent this, four separate discriminators $D_k$ are assigned to four horizontal quadrants (forward, backward, left, right). The discriminator aligned with the intended root escape vector is activated to regularize the policy against a dataset of 90 human dodging motions. This allows the policy to reliably learn aggressive evasions like forward duck-steps.

### III-D Training Details
Policies were trained with PPO across 4,096 parallel environments in the "mjlab" simulator for both Unitree G1 and EngineAI PM01. Obstacle trajectories include straight paths and randomized gravitational parabolas with extensive domain randomization across launch speeds and target links. The actor network processes a 20-step observation history through a 1D CNN, enabling latent velocity inference without explicit projectile velocity inputs.

captions.F2: The overall pipeline. Sphere-based threat calculation arbitrates between evasion rewards and capture point recovery rewards, while direction-specific AMP discriminators encourage natural motions conditioned on the root evasion heading. The policy transfers zero-shot to hardware using projectile coordinates from motion capture.

sections.heading: Staying standing against brutal trajectories: Crushing baselines in simulation
sections.summary: Evaluated across 2,304 obstacle configurations on both G1 and PM01, the proposed method consistently surpassed baselines (PAC-MAN, REBot) in dodge success rate. Direction-specific AMP enabled balanced multi-directional maneuvers, and the capture point reward drastically reduced fall rates.
sections.details:
### IV-A Benchmark Setup and Baselines
The benchmark evaluates 2,304 unique settings covering obstacle initial speeds (4–15 m/s), 16 launch azimuths, and launch distances (1.0–6.5 m), running 100 trials per setting. Baselines include REBot (reflexive quadruped avoidance ported to humanoids) and PAC-MAN (a concurrent CBF + AMP humanoid evasion approach).

### IV-B Evasion Performance
Across all bins of time-to-hit ($\mathrm{TTH} = \text{distance} / \text{velocity}$), the proposed method achieved the highest success rates. In scenarios with ample reaction time ($\mathrm{TTH} \ge 1.2\,\mathrm{s}$), where REBot plateaued around 50% and PAC-MAN reached 70–80%, the proposed method achieved 96.8% on G1 and 93.6% on PM01.

Directional heatmaps reveal that while PAC-MAN suffers significant blind spots against frontal and rear projectiles, the proposed method maintains uniformly high success in all directions. Hit distribution analysis showed PAC-MAN frequently incurred direct torso and head hits, whereas the proposed method reduced upper-body impacts dramatically, with most remaining contacts confined to the feet (which are constrained as ground supports). However, due to faster, more aggressive maneuvers, the average power consumption was higher than that of PAC-MAN.

### IV-C Motion Diversity Analysis
t-SNE visualizations of evasive trajectories revealed that PAC-MAN almost exclusively collapses into backward retreating, and a single-AMP variant also rarely generated forward dodges. In contrast, the proposed 4-direction AMP evenly dispersed motions across all four quadrants, showing that the robot dynamically chooses between varied stepping and ducking strategies.

### IV-D Ablation Studies
Removing individual reward terms demonstrated that omitting distance clearance $r^{\mathrm{distance}}$ or escape velocity $r^{\mathrm{escape}}$ severely degraded performance under short reaction windows ($\mathrm{TTH} < 1.0\,\mathrm{s}$). Removing the capture point reward $r^{\mathrm{capture}}$ caused fall rates to jump from under 1% to around 4%, and reverting to a single AMP discriminator worsened the fall rate to nearly 10%. These ablations confirm that both components are indispensable for agility and stability.

captions.F3: Evasion success rate heatmaps. In the polar plots (top), the proposed method (right) demonstrates complete omnidirectional coverage compared to PAC-MAN (left). In the distance-velocity plots (bottom), the 60% success boundary (red line) is pushed into much faster, shorter-range regimes.
captions.F5: t-SNE visualization of evasive maneuvers. PAC-MAN (right) and single-AMP (center) collapse into backward retreats (red), whereas the proposed method (left) exhibits a well-balanced distribution across all directions (forward: blue, backward: red, left: green, right: orange), confirming a rich behavioral repertoire.
captions.F6: Ablation study results. (a) Removing reward components degrades success rates, especially at low time-to-hit (TTH). (b) Omitting the capture point reward (orange) or using a single AMP discriminator (green) sharply increases fall rates.

sections.heading: Real PM01 deployment: Evading 36 km/h balls with steps and ducks
sections.summary: Using an EngineAI PM01 robot with real-time motion capture tracking, projectile evasion experiments were conducted. Facing balls launched at 3.0 to 10 m/s, the robot achieved a 73% success rate (22 of 30 trials), proving that whole-body forward steps, side steps, and ducking transfer reliably to the physical world.
sections.details:
The simulation-trained policy was deployed zero-shot onto an EngineAI PM01 humanoid. A ball (0.12 m radius) and the robot were tracked by an external motion capture system, streaming the ball's relative position in the robot base frame to the policy.

In experiments, balls were thrown at the robot from various angles at speeds between 3.0 and 10 m/s (roughly 11 to 36 km/h). The robot reacted by executing diverse whole-body evasive maneuvers:
- Stepping forward to evade a ball targeting the frontal torso
- Deep ducking combined with a forward step to dodge a head-level projectile
- Side-stepping to the left against a shot aimed at the right shoulder
- Simultaneously stepping right and ducking against a high pitch

Out of 30 physical trials, the robot successfully evaded the projectile and recovered to a stable standing posture in 22 attempts (an overall success rate of ~73%).

Among the 8 failed trials, 6 were direct ball hits and 2 were falls during motion execution. Most direct hits occurred on pitches thrown directly at the torso at speeds exceeding 8 m/s, where the robot began evasive motion but could not physically finish before impact. A specific failure mode involved low ground-level balls, where the robot's swinging leg struck the ball during a lateral step. Despite these edge cases and the sim-to-real gap, achieving such agile, whole-body coordinated stepping on hardware represents a significant step forward.

captions.F7: Time-lapse sequences of physical evasion trials on EngineAI PM01. (a) Forward step, (b) forward step with ducking, (c) left side-step, and (d) right step with ducking, showing flexible, human-like dodging strategies adapted to projectile height and trajectory.

sections.heading: Takeaways and future work: Moving toward onboard perception and integrated tasks
sections.summary: By unifying threat-aware rewards, directional AMP, and capture point control, high-speed dynamic obstacle evasion was demonstrated in simulation and on real hardware. Future work will eliminate motion capture dependencies, transition to onboard vision and sensing, and integrate evasion into ongoing locomotion and manipulation tasks.
sections.details:
This work presented "Humanoid Dodgeball," an agile control framework enabling humanoids to dodge incoming projectiles. Extensive experiments across simulation (G1, PM01) and real hardware (PM01) verified superior evasion success and postural recovery compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Several limitations remain for real-world deployment:
- Ultra-high-speed projectiles: When reaction time is extremely short ($\mathrm{TTH} < 0.4\,\mathrm{s}$), the robot cannot evade in time due to hardware actuator limits.
- Energy trade-offs: Compared to PAC-MAN, the policy achieves higher dodge rates through aggressive steps, resulting in higher average motor power consumption.
- Reliance on external tracking: Real-world experiments rely on external motion capture for ball state estimation; onboard vision or LiDAR will be required for standalone deployment.

Future work will focus on closing the sim-to-real gap through advanced actuator dynamics modeling, handling multiple concurrent obstacles, and developing unified policies that dodge projectiles during routine walking or load-carrying tasks.

takeaways: When generating diverse behaviors with AMP, partitioning discriminators by intended escape direction (Direction-Specific AMP) is far more effective than relying on a single monolithic discriminator.

In aggressive whole-body evasion RL, blending classical balance metrics like capture points (from the linear inverted pendulum model) with geometric avoidance rewards strongly suppresses post-maneuver falls.

Modeling the body and projectile as bounding spheres to evaluate online "time-to-collision" and "required acceleration" provides a lightweight yet accurate supervision signal for localized link evasion.
limitations: Hardware deployment currently relies on an external motion capture system to track projectile positions; fully autonomous evasion using only onboard perception has not yet been demonstrated.
To maximize dodge success, the policy relies on dynamic multi-step maneuvers, which incur higher motor power consumption and longer post-dodge recovery times compared to baselines like PAC-MAN.
For low-rolling obstacles near the feet, evasion freedom is heavily constrained by balance support needs, occasionally causing the swinging leg to hit the obstacle during steps.
